summary:
Región de Los Ríos stands under Chile's national framework, and Outright International's Chile country dossier, published 12 March 2026, carries no Los Ríos-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding. What a trans visitor encounters in this region is therefore what Chilean law provides nationwide.

Legal gender recognition rests on Gender Identity Law 21,120, in force since 27 December 2019. Adults may change their registered name and sex on request to the Civil Registry without therapy or surgery. Applicants aged 14 to 18 must apply to family courts with psychosocial and family-context antecedents, and people under 14 cannot use the law, although the statute recognises them as transgender. On 9 April 2025 the Constitutional Court declared the 'over 14 years old' wording inapplicable as unconstitutional in a case brought by the mother of a 10-year-old trans girl, with the ruling confined to that case.

The 2012 Zamudio Law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity, was extended to gender expression in 2018, and treats hate-crime motivation as an aggravating criminal circumstance. Same-sex marriage and joint adoption have been legal since March 2022, civil unions since 2015, and birth certificates offer a third sex option for intersex children since 2006.

Transphobic violence remains documented. A young trans man was murdered in 2023 in a killing covered up for 24 hours and described in national reporting as Chile's largest hate crime; the perpetrator, an acquaintance, confessed. In September 2021 a 20-year-old trans man and his girlfriend were beaten with bottles and clubs and held against their will for close to an hour at a Santiago hotel, where the attacker said he wanted to kill the victim.

Entry and removal rules reference gender identity. The Migration and Immigration Law of 11 April 2021 bans arbitrary discrimination based on sexual orientation and gender identity and offers protection to LGBT immigrants seeking asylum. Article 10 provides that recognised asylum seekers may be granted complementary protection, and no foreigner holding complementary protection may be expelled or returned to a country where their right to life, physical integrity or personal freedom is at risk on grounds including sexual orientation or gender identity.

Los Ríos accounts for 1.04% of nationally documented abuse cases in Movilh's XXIV annual report (HECHOS 2025), published March 2026, a rise of 14.28% year-on-year in 2025. Nationally the report counts 3,620 cases and complaints of discrimination in 2025, up 27.1% and the highest in 24 years. Only Valparaíso and Metropolitana fell, by 17.56% and 14.35%, while the other 14 regions rose. Movilh reads the shift as hatred expanding into regions with less public debate, which supports a mid-level risk assessment for Los Ríos.

Detention carries specific rules. Gendarmería de Chile's national director signed a protocol guaranteeing the gender identity of trans detainees, providing placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations, with a standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives overseeing implementation, including access rules for trans visitors.
tangentialFactors:
Restrictive proposals are active in Chile but non-binding on the region. On 15 May 2025 the Chamber of Deputies approved the CEI 57 commission report, 56 votes to 30 with 6 abstentions, a non-binding recommendation to eliminate the Gender Identity Support Program, restrict minors' progressive autonomy, ban hormonal treatment for minors and repeal the circular protecting gender identity in schools.

The 2025-26 rollback reached the budget. In November 2025 Congress defunded the Ministry of Social Development's Gender Identity Support Program through the 2026 Budget Law, an action condemned by civil society groups and the national ombuds for children. On 9 January 2025 the Constitutional Court, by seven votes to three, annulled section 46 of the 2025 Budget Law, which had barred the Ministry of Health from financing hormone therapies for trans children and adolescents.

Circular 7 of June 2024 from the health authorities suggested deferring the initiation of new gonadotropin-releasing hormone blockers and cross-sex hormone therapy in adolescents until national guidelines are published; the Medical College noted that physicians may still prescribe.

Regional movement is uneven across Chile. Los Ríos rose 14.28% in documented abuse cases during 2025 while Valparaíso fell 17.56% and Metropolitana fell 14.35%, leaving the direction of travel in Los Ríos contrary to the two largest metropolitan regions.
localsOnly:
The public health system has funded sex reassignment surgery and hormone therapy since 2013, and a 2011 Ministry of Health circular obliges all care centres to register transgender patients by their social name. Although the Ministry of Social Development's programme lost its funding through the 2026 Budget Law, the Ministry of Health-run programme continues to provide support in medical centres, and the Crece con Orgullo programme has operated since 2023 for children and adolescents aged 3 to 17.

Residents held in custody fall under the Gendarmería de Chile protocol on gender identity, which provides placement by assumed gender, segmented housing and entry examinations. A standing committee of Gendarmería and undersecretariat representatives oversees implementation, and the protocol includes rules on access for trans visitors.

Residents of Los Ríos appear in Movilh's national abuse statistics at a 1.04% share, with documented cases in the region rising 14.28% in 2025 against a national total of 3,620 cases and complaints, an increase of 27.1% and the highest figure in 24 years.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Los Ríos-specific legal, incident or enforcement finding appears in Outright International's Chile country dossier of 12 March 2026, so the regional assessment rests on national law and on Movilh's regional share of abuse cases; region-level judicial, policing or service-delivery material is unresolved for this profile.

Movilh's 2025 edition does not state the Los Ríos share for 2024, so the comparison behind the reported 14.28% year-on-year rise cannot be verified from that source alone.

The Constitutional Court ruling of 9 April 2025 on the 'over 14 years old' wording applies only to the case before it, and the CEI 57 commission report approved on 15 May 2025 is a non-binding recommendation; neither changes the standing national rules as written.
